The word rafter has two separate meanings as a noun. The first is the common, everyday meaning used in construction and architecture. The second is a more specialized meaning used in nature and wildlife.
Meaning 1: A sloping beam in a roof

This is by far the most common meaning of "rafter."

A rafter is one of the long, sloping beams — usually made of wood, steel, or concrete — that form the inner frame of a slanted roof. Think of rafters as the "skeleton" of a roof. They start at the top (the pointed peak of the roof, called the ridge) and slope downward on both sides to the walls of the building. The actual outer surface of the roof — the tiles, shingles, or metal sheets you see from outside — sits on top of the rafters and is supported by them.

A simple way to picture it: Imagine a tent. The tent poles that go from the top peak downward and outward, giving the tent its triangular shape? Rafters play a similar role in a building's roof, except they are much more solid and structural.

In a typical house with a slanted roof, there are many rafters placed parallel to each other, side by side, running from one end of the building to the other. Together, they form the entire sloping framework of the roof.

What rafters do:

  • They carry the weight of the roof covering (tiles, shingles, snow, etc.)
  • They give the roof its shape and slope
  • They transfer that weight down to the walls of the building

You would typically hear this word in construction, carpentry, and architecture:

  • "The carpenter nailed the roof tiles to the rafters."
  • "After the storm, one of the rafters cracked under the weight of the snow."
  • "They left the rafters exposed, giving the ceiling a rustic, wooden look."

That last example is worth noting. In some homes, barns, or restaurants, the rafters are intentionally left visible from inside — you look up at the ceiling and can see the wooden beams slanting upward. This is called an exposed-rafter ceiling, and it is considered an aesthetic choice.

This is a much lesser-known meaning, but it is perfectly valid and worth knowing.

A rafter is the collective noun for a group of wild turkeys. Just as you say "a flock of birds" or "a herd of cows," you say "a rafter of turkeys."

  • "A rafter of turkeys wandered through the field."

This usage is mostly encountered in wildlife writing, nature documentaries, and hunting contexts. In everyday conversation, most people simply say "a flock of turkeys" and would be just as correct.

Rafter (construction)A sloping beam that forms the inner framework of a roof, running from the peak down to the walls
Rafter (wildlife)A collective noun for a group of wild turkeys

The construction meaning is the one you will encounter in the vast majority of situations. If someone says "rafter" without any context about animals or wildlife, they almost certainly mean the roof beam.
